title: Harvesting losses and gains
teaches: Selling at a loss to bank a deduction, the wash-sale rule, choosing which lots to sell, and selling at a gain in years when the rate is 0 percent

blocks.text: A taxable account's tax depends on when its gains and losses are realised, and its owner chooses when. Two techniques use that choice. Loss harvesting sells holdings that have fallen, to bank a loss for the tax return, and buys something similar so the portfolio barely changes. Gain harvesting, met in lesson 10, sells holdings that have risen in a year when the gain is taxed at 0 percent, and buys them straight back to raise the basis.
Both trades leave the portfolio as it was. What they change is the basis, and with it the tax due later.

Realised losses first cancel realised gains of the same year. Any loss left over reduces ordinary income by up to $3,000 a year, and whatever remains carries forward without limit, to future years' gains or $3,000 a year of income.[^order]

Suppose an index fund bought for $50,000 is worth $40,000 after a fall. Selling it and buying a similar fund books a $10,000 loss. The new fund's basis is $40,000, so if it recovers to $50,000 there is now a $10,000 gain where there would have been none. The loss today is paid back by a gain later.

So harvesting a loss is worth the difference between the rate it saves now and the rate the extra gain pays later, plus the use of the money in between. Where the loss offsets ordinary income at 22 percent and the gain is later taxed at 15, each $10,000 is worth $700. Where the extra gain is never taxed, because the shares are held until death or given to charity, the whole saving is kept.

blocks.text: A loss is disallowed if the same or a substantially identical security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale. The disallowed loss isn't lost, only postponed: it is added to the basis of the new purchase. But a purchase inside an IRA or Roth, including a reinvested dividend, counts too, and there the loss is gone for good.[^ira-wash]

The usual way through is to switch between two funds that track different indexes of the same market, such as a total US market fund and an S&P 500 fund. Their returns are nearly identical; whether they are substantially identical has never been ruled on, and the common practice is to treat different indexes as different.[^identical] Switching off automatic dividend reinvestment around the sale avoids small accidental wash sales.

Shares bought at different times are different lots, each with its own basis. When selling part of a holding, the seller can name which lots go. Choosing the lots with the highest basis, and those held more than a year, keeps the taxable gain smallest. Most brokers default to first in, first out, which usually sells the oldest, cheapest lots first; changing the default to specific identification is a one-time setting.

Gain harvesting is the mirror image. A couple whose taxable income is under $98,900 in 2026 pays 0 percent on long-term gains up to that line. Selling winners and buying them back the same day realises the gain at 0 percent and raises the basis, with no wash-sale problem, because the rule only applies to losses. The two harvests compete: a carried-forward loss is used up against gains first, so a household planning to harvest gains at 0 percent gets less from its banked losses, which would otherwise have been used against income.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A harvested loss lowers basis: it is worth the rate saved now minus the rate the extra gain pays later.
Losses offset gains, then $3,000 a year of income, and carry forward without limit.
Buying the same or a substantially identical fund within 30 days, including in an IRA, triggers the wash-sale rule.
Name the lots you sell: high basis and long-term first.
In years under the 0 percent line, harvest gains instead: sell and rebuy at once to raise the basis tax-free.

blocks.caption: Five questions on harvesting
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A $10,000 loss offsets $10,000 of long-term gains taxed at 15 percent, and the replacement fund is later sold at a gain taxed at 15 percent. What has the harvest gained?
choices: Only the deferral of the tax
items.why: The lower basis creates an equal extra gain at the same rate later.

items.ask: How much of a net capital loss can reduce ordinary income in one year?
items.why: Up to $3,000 a year against income, and the remainder carries forward indefinitely.

items.ask: You sell a fund at a loss in your brokerage account and your IRA reinvests a dividend into the same fund a week later. What happens?
choices: Part of the loss is disallowed permanently
items.why: A purchase in an IRA triggers a wash sale, and the basis can't be added to an IRA, so that part of the loss is lost.

items.ask: Why does a wash sale not apply to gain harvesting?
choices: The rule covers only sales at a loss
Gains are always taxed at 0 percent
Gain harvesting is done inside an IRA
items.why: Selling at a gain and rebuying at once is allowed; it simply raises the basis.

items.ask: When does a harvested loss become a permanent saving?
choices: When the extra gain is never taxed, for example shares held until death
items.why: The step-up at death or a gift to charity erases the gain the harvest created.

summary: **Harvesting changes the basis, not the portfolio.** Sell and replace, so the holdings stay the same.
**A loss is a loan from the future.** It lowers basis, so its worth is the rate saved now minus the rate paid later.
**Losses offset gains, then $3,000 of income.** The rest carries forward without limit.
**Watch the wash-sale rule.** 30 days either side, IRAs included; switch to a fund on a different index.
**Choose the lots.** Selling high-basis, long-term lots keeps the gain smallest.
**Harvest gains in 0 percent years.** Sell and rebuy at once to raise the basis tax-free.

order.title: The netting order
order.text: Short-term losses first offset short-term gains and long-term losses long-term gains; then any net loss of one kind offsets the other. A carried-forward loss keeps its character, short or long. Short-term losses are the more valuable, since short-term gains are taxed at ordinary rates.

identical.title: Substantially identical
identical.text: The IRS has never defined the phrase for funds. Shares of the same fund, or a fund's ETF and mutual fund classes, are plainly identical. Two funds from different companies on the same index are argued both ways; funds on different indexes are generally treated as different. Automated harvesting services rely on that reading.

ira-wash.title: IRAs, spouses and the 61-day window
ira-wash.text: The window is 30 calendar days before the sale, the day of the sale, and 30 calendar days after: 61 days in all. In Revenue Ruling 2008-5, the IRS ruled that buying the replacement shares in a traditional or Roth IRA disallows the loss without increasing the IRA's basis, so the deduction vanishes. Purchases by a spouse, or by a company the seller controls, count as well.
